Genesis.author: Traditionally Moses; most modern scholars see edited earlier sources compiled by the exilic period
Genesis.date: Events c. 2000–1600 BC (patriarchs); composition traditionally 15th c. BC, final form no later than 5th c. BC
Genesis.audience: Israel on the edge of the promised land, needing to know who their God is and where they came from
Genesis.setting: Mesopotamia, Canaan and Egypt in the Middle Bronze Age; a world of city-states, clan migration and covenant treaties
Genesis.purpose: To ground Israel's identity in the God who created the world, chose Abraham, and kept his promises through failure and famine
themes: Promise of land, seed and blessing
outline: Primeval history: creation, fall, flood, Babel
Joseph and the move to Egypt

Exodus.author: Traditionally Moses
Exodus.date: Exodus c. 1491 BC (Ussher, as dated here); others c. 1446 BC (early) or c. 1270 BC (late)
Exodus.audience: The generation of Israel formed into a nation at Sinai
Exodus.setting: New Kingdom Egypt (a pharaoh of the 18th or 19th dynasty), the Sinai wilderness
Exodus.purpose: To show how YHWH redeemed Israel from slavery, bound them to himself by covenant, and came to dwell among them
outline: Tabernacle instructions, golden calf, tabernacle built

Leviticus.author: Traditionally Moses
Leviticus.date: Received at Sinai, c. 1490 BC (Ussher); others c. 1446 or 1270 BC
Leviticus.audience: Priests and people of Israel camped at Sinai
Leviticus.setting: The newly built tabernacle; a holy God now dwells in the middle of the camp
Leviticus.purpose: To teach how sinful people can live in the presence of a holy God through sacrifice, priesthood and holiness

Numbers.author: Traditionally Moses
Numbers.date: Events c. 1490–1451 BC (Ussher); others c. 1446–1406 or 1270–1230 BC
Numbers.audience: The second wilderness generation about to enter Canaan
Numbers.setting: Forty years of wandering from Sinai to the plains of Moab
Numbers.purpose: To record the failure of the first generation and God's faithfulness in preparing the second
outline: New generation prepares for the land

Deuteronomy.author: Traditionally Moses (final chapter added later)
Deuteronomy.date: Plains of Moab, c. 1451 BC (Ussher; others c. 1406 or 1230 BC); many scholars date the final form to the 7th c. BC
Deuteronomy.audience: Israel about to cross the Jordan without Moses
Deuteronomy.setting: Moab, east of the Jordan; structured like an ancient Near-Eastern suzerain–vassal treaty
Deuteronomy.purpose: To renew the covenant and call a new generation to love and obey YHWH in the land
themes: Love the LORD with all your heart (the Shema)

Joshua.author: Anonymous; tradition associates it with Joshua and later editors
Joshua.date: Events c. 1451–1427 BC (Ussher); others c. 1406–1380 BC or 13th c. BC
Joshua.audience: Israel settled in the land, remembering how it was given
Joshua.setting: Late Bronze Age Canaan: fortified city-states in decline, Egyptian influence waning
Joshua.purpose: To show God keeping his land promise and to call Israel to faithful covenant loyalty

Judges.author: Anonymous; tradition suggests Samuel
Judges.date: Events c. 1420–1120 BC (Ussher); others c. 1380–1050 BC
Judges.setting: Tribal Israel with no central government, pressured by Canaanites, Midianites and Philistines
Judges.purpose: To show the downward spiral of a people who do what is right in their own eyes, and God's repeated mercy
themes: Cycle of sin, oppression, cry, deliverance
Israel's need for a righteous king

Ruth.author: Anonymous
Ruth.date: Set in the judges period, c. 1308 BC (Ussher); others c. 1100 BC; written during or after David's reign
Ruth.audience: Israel in the monarchy, curious about David's Moabite roots
Ruth.setting: Bethlehem and Moab during a famine; agricultural life, kinsman-redeemer customs
Ruth.purpose: To show God's hidden providence and covenant loyalty (hesed) working through ordinary faithfulness, and to trace David's line

1 Samuel.author: Anonymous; tradition points to Samuel, Nathan and Gad
1 Samuel.date: Events c. 1165–1056 BC (Ussher); others c. 1100–1010 BC
1 Samuel.audience: Israel reflecting on the birth of the monarchy
1 Samuel.setting: Transition from judges to kings under Philistine pressure
1 Samuel.purpose: To show how Israel got a king and why God rejected Saul and chose David
themes: The LORD looks at the heart

2 Samuel.author: Anonymous; tradition points to Nathan and Gad
2 Samuel.date: Events c. 1055–1015 BC (Ussher); others c. 1010–970 BC
2 Samuel.setting: David's reign: Jerusalem captured, kingdom united and expanded
2 Samuel.purpose: To narrate David's reign honestly—his triumphs, God's covenant with him, and the consequences of his sin
themes: God's grace to a flawed king
outline: Sin with Bathsheba and family turmoil

1 Kings.author: Anonymous (tradition: Jeremiah); compiled from court records and prophetic sources
1 Kings.date: Events c. 1015–897 BC (Ussher); others c. 970–850 BC; final form in the exile (after 560 BC)
1 Kings.audience: Exiles asking why the kingdom fell
1 Kings.setting: Solomon's empire, then the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah
1 Kings.purpose: To evaluate each king by covenant faithfulness and explain the road to exile

2 Kings.author: Anonymous (tradition: Jeremiah)
2 Kings.date: Events c. 896–562 BC (Ussher); others c. 850–560 BC
2 Kings.setting: Assyrian conquest of Israel (722 BC), Babylonian conquest of Judah (586 BC)
2 Kings.purpose: To show that exile was covenant judgement, yet leave a flicker of hope in the Davidic line
outline: Judah's last kings and fall of Jerusalem

1 Chronicles.author: Anonymous 'the Chronicler' (tradition: Ezra)
1 Chronicles.audience: Post-exilic community rebuilding identity around temple and Davidic hope
1 Chronicles.setting: Persian-period Judah, a small province around a rebuilt temple
1 Chronicles.purpose: To retell Israel's story emphasising David, worship and continuity with the past

2 Chronicles.author: The Chronicler
2 Chronicles.setting: Same as 1 Chronicles; covers Solomon to the decree of Cyrus
2 Chronicles.purpose: To highlight temple worship and show that seeking God brings blessing, forsaking him brings ruin
outline: Kings of Judah to the exile and Cyrus' decree

Ezra.author: Traditionally Ezra
Ezra.setting: Persian empire; Cyrus' decree allowing return; rebuilding the temple amid opposition
Ezra.purpose: To record the return and restoration of worship and the covenant community
outline: First return under Zerubbabel; temple rebuilt

Nehemiah.author: Nehemiah's memoirs, compiled with Ezra
Nehemiah.setting: Persian province of Yehud; Nehemiah as governor under Artaxerxes I
Nehemiah.purpose: To show God rebuilding walls and people through prayer, leadership and covenant renewal

Esther.author: Anonymous Jewish author in Persia
Esther.date: Events c. 462–452 BC (Ussher); others c. 483–473 BC; written late 5th or 4th c. BC
Esther.setting: Persian court at Susa under Xerxes I (Ahasuerus)
Esther.purpose: To show God's hidden providence preserving his people and to explain Purim
themes: Courage ('for such a time as this')

Job.author: Anonymous
Job.date: Events set in the patriarchal era; date of composition debated (Solomonic to post-exilic)
Job.audience: Wisdom seekers wrestling with innocent suffering
Job.setting: Land of Uz (Edom region); a non-Israelite sage
Job.purpose: To confront simplistic retribution theology and point to trust in God's wisdom amid unexplained suffering
outline: Prologue: the LORD allows Job to be tested

Psalms.author: David (73), Asaph, sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses, and anonymous writers
Psalms.date: c. 1490–400 BC; collected in five books after the exile
Psalms.audience: Israel at worship, and every individual before God
Psalms.setting: Temple worship, royal court, personal crisis, exile
Psalms.purpose: To give words for every season of faith—praise, lament, thanksgiving, wisdom, kingship

Proverbs.author: Solomon mainly; also Agur, Lemuel, 'the wise'; edited under Hezekiah
Proverbs.audience: Young people learning to navigate life
Proverbs.setting: Royal court and household instruction in Israel's wisdom tradition
Proverbs.purpose: To impart skill for living rooted in the fear of the LORD

Ecclesiastes.author: 'Qoheleth' (the Teacher), traditionally Solomon
Ecclesiastes.date: c. 1000–975 BC if Solomonic; language suggests to many a later date (5th–3rd c. BC)
Ecclesiastes.setting: Wisdom reflection on life 'under the sun'
Ecclesiastes.purpose: To expose the vanity of life without God and call for reverent enjoyment and obedience
themes: Fear God and keep his commandments

Song of Songs.author: Associated with Solomon
Song of Songs.audience: Israel celebrating covenant love and marriage
Song of Songs.setting: Pastoral and royal imagery of ancient Israel
Song of Songs.purpose: To celebrate love, desire and faithfulness between bride and groom; read also as Christ and his people

Isaiah.author: Isaiah son of Amoz (many scholars see chs. 40–66 as later disciples)
Isaiah.audience: Judah under Assyrian threat, and future exiles
Isaiah.setting: Reigns of Uzziah to Hezekiah; Assyria's rise, siege of Jerusalem 701 BC
Isaiah.purpose: To call Judah to trust the Holy One of Israel and to announce judgement, exile and glorious restoration through the Servant

Jeremiah.author: Jeremiah, with scribe Baruch
Jeremiah.audience: Judah in its final decades and the first exiles
Jeremiah.setting: Josiah's reform, Babylon's rise, fall of Jerusalem 586 BC
Jeremiah.purpose: To call for repentance, announce inevitable judgement, and promise a new covenant

Lamentations.author: Traditionally Jeremiah
Lamentations.setting: Ruined Jerusalem; five laments, the first four alphabetic acrostics
Lamentations.purpose: To grieve honestly before God while confessing his faithfulness
outline: Hope in the midst of grief

Ezekiel.author: Ezekiel, priest and prophet
Ezekiel.setting: Jewish community by the Chebar canal in Babylon, before and after Jerusalem's fall
Ezekiel.purpose: To show God's glory leaving the temple in judgement and returning in restoration

Daniel.author: Daniel (many scholars date final form to 2nd c. BC)
Daniel.purpose: To show God's sovereignty over empires and encourage faithfulness under pressure
themes: God rules the kingdoms of men
outline: Narrative: Daniel and his friends in the Babylonian and Persian courts

Hosea.author: Hosea
Hosea.setting: Israel's prosperity and decline before Assyria's conquest
Hosea.purpose: To portray Israel's spiritual adultery and God's relentless covenant love

Joel.author: Joel son of Pethuel
Joel.date: Uncertain: 9th c. BC or post-exilic (c. 500–400 BC)
Joel.audience: Judah after a devastating locust plague
Joel.setting: Agricultural catastrophe as a foretaste of the Day of the LORD
Joel.purpose: To call for repentance and promise the outpouring of the Spirit
outline: Call to repent; promise of Spirit

Amos.author: Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa
Amos.audience: Prosperous northern Israel under Jeroboam II
Amos.setting: Economic boom, social injustice, religious complacency
Amos.purpose: To denounce injustice and empty worship and announce judgement

Obadiah.author: Obadiah
Obadiah.date: After Jerusalem's fall, c. 586–550 BC (some argue 9th c.)
Obadiah.purpose: To announce judgement on Edom and the restoration of Israel
outline: Day of the LORD and Zion

Jonah.author: Anonymous; about Jonah son of Amittai
Jonah.date: Events c. 825 BC (Ussher, under Jeroboam II, 2 Kgs 14:25); others c. 780–750 BC
Jonah.audience: Israel resistant to God's mercy on enemies
Jonah.setting: Nineveh, capital of Assyria; a great fish
Jonah.purpose: To expose narrow nationalism and reveal God's compassion for all nations

Micah.author: Micah of Moresheth
Micah.setting: Assyrian crisis; corrupt leaders in Samaria and Jerusalem
Micah.purpose: To indict injustice and promise a ruler from Bethlehem

Nahum.author: Nahum of Elkosh
Nahum.purpose: To announce the downfall of cruel Nineveh

Habakkuk.author: Habakkuk
Habakkuk.setting: Injustice in Judah; Babylon's approaching conquest
Habakkuk.purpose: To wrestle with why God uses the wicked and to affirm that the righteous live by faith
themes: The just shall live by faith (2:4)

Zephaniah.author: Zephaniah, descendant of Hezekiah
Zephaniah.purpose: To warn of the Day of the LORD and promise a purified remnant

Haggai.author: Haggai
Haggai.setting: Persian period; second year of Darius
Haggai.purpose: To rouse the people to rebuild the temple

Zechariah.author: Zechariah son of Berechiah
Zechariah.setting: Rebuilding of the temple; Persian rule
Zechariah.purpose: To encourage rebuilding and to unveil the coming Messianic king and kingdom

Malachi.author: Malachi ('my messenger')
Malachi.setting: Temple rebuilt but worship half-hearted; last prophetic voice before 400 silent years
Malachi.purpose: To confront apathy and promise the coming messenger and Day of the LORD
outline: Messenger and Day of the LORD

Matthew.author: Traditionally Matthew (Levi), the tax collector apostle
Matthew.setting: Roman-occupied Judea and Galilee; synagogue and church parting ways
Matthew.purpose: To present Jesus as the Messiah who fulfils the Law and Prophets and founds the church

Mark.author: John Mark, associate of Peter
Mark.setting: Rome under Nero, likely; fast-paced narrative for Gentile readers
Mark.purpose: To present Jesus as the suffering Son of God and Servant who gives his life as a ransom

Luke.author: Luke, physician and companion of Paul
Luke.purpose: To give an orderly account showing Jesus as Saviour for all people, especially the marginalised

John.author: Traditionally John the apostle, 'the disciple whom Jesus loved'
John.audience: Broad: Jews and Greeks, believers and seekers
John.setting: Ephesus, late first century; synagogue tension and early heresies
John.purpose: That you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (20:31)

Acts.author: Luke
Acts.setting: Jerusalem to Rome across the empire, AD 30–62
Acts.purpose: To narrate the Spirit-empowered spread of the gospel from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth

Romans.author: Paul
Romans.date: c. AD 60, from Corinth (Ussher); others c. AD 57
Romans.audience: House churches in Rome, Jewish and Gentile
Romans.setting: Paul preparing to visit Rome en route to Spain; tension between Jewish and Gentile believers
Romans.purpose: To set out the gospel of righteousness by faith for Jew and Gentile alike

1 Corinthians.author: Paul
1 Corinthians.date: c. AD 59, from Ephesus (Ussher); others c. AD 53–55
1 Corinthians.setting: Wealthy, immoral port city; a divided, gifted, immature church
1 Corinthians.purpose: To correct divisions and disorders and call the church to the way of the cross and love

2 Corinthians.author: Paul
2 Corinthians.date: c. AD 60, from Macedonia (Ussher); others c. AD 55–56
2 Corinthians.setting: After a painful visit and letter; opponents challenging Paul's authority
2 Corinthians.purpose: To defend Paul's apostolic ministry and encourage reconciliation and generosity

Galatians.author: Paul
Galatians.purpose: To defend justification by faith apart from works of the law

Ephesians.author: Paul (some scholars propose a disciple)
Ephesians.date: c. AD 64, from prison in Rome (Ussher); others c. AD 60–62
Ephesians.setting: Diverse Jew–Gentile congregations in a city of magic and pagan worship
Ephesians.purpose: To unfold God's eternal plan in Christ and the unity and holiness of the church

Philippians.author: Paul
Philippians.date: c. AD 64, from prison in Rome (Ussher); others c. AD 60–62
Philippians.audience: Church in Philippi, a Roman colony
Philippians.setting: Paul imprisoned; the church facing opposition and internal friction
Philippians.purpose: To thank the church and call them to joyful, humble unity in Christ

Colossians.author: Paul
Colossians.date: c. AD 64, from prison in Rome (Ussher); others c. AD 60–62
Colossians.setting: A church tempted by a syncretistic philosophy of asceticism and ritual
Colossians.purpose: To show the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ
themes: Christ the image of the invisible God

1 Thessalonians.author: Paul (with Silas and Timothy)
1 Thessalonians.date: c. AD 54, from Corinth (Ussher); others c. AD 50–51; one of the earliest NT books
1 Thessalonians.purpose: To encourage a young church and clarify the return of Christ

2 Thessalonians.author: Paul
2 Thessalonians.date: c. AD 54, from Corinth (Ussher); others c. AD 51
2 Thessalonians.setting: Confusion that the Day of the Lord had already come
2 Thessalonians.purpose: To correct end-time misunderstanding and confront idleness

1 Timothy.author: Paul (authorship of the Pastorals debated)
1 Timothy.audience: Timothy, leading the church at Ephesus
1 Timothy.setting: False teaching, leadership disorder in Ephesus
1 Timothy.purpose: To instruct on sound doctrine, church order and godly leadership

2 Timothy.author: Paul
2 Timothy.date: c. AD 64–67, from Roman prison before execution
2 Timothy.setting: Paul's final letter; desertion by many; Nero's persecution
2 Timothy.purpose: To urge Timothy to guard the gospel and endure hardship

Titus.author: Paul
Titus.setting: Crete's reputation for dishonesty; new churches needing elders
Titus.purpose: To set the churches in order and show how grace produces good works

Philemon.author: Paul
Philemon.date: c. AD 64, from prison in Rome (Ussher); others c. AD 60–62
Philemon.setting: Onesimus, Philemon's runaway slave, converted under Paul
Philemon.purpose: To appeal for Onesimus to be received as a brother

Hebrews.author: Anonymous (suggestions: Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, Luke)
Hebrews.audience: Jewish Christians tempted to drift back to Judaism
Hebrews.setting: Pressure and persecution; temple still functioning
Hebrews.purpose: To show Christ's superiority over Moses, priests and sacrifices, and to call for perseverance
outline: The Son supreme, greater than Moses

James.author: James, brother of Jesus, leader in Jerusalem
James.setting: Diaspora believers facing trials, poverty and partiality
James.purpose: To call for practical, wholehearted faith that works

1 Peter.author: Peter (with Silvanus)
1 Peter.setting: Social hostility and scattered exiles under Roman rule
1 Peter.purpose: To encourage suffering believers to live as holy exiles with hope

2 Peter.author: Peter (authorship widely debated)
2 Peter.setting: False teachers mocking the promise of Christ's return
2 Peter.purpose: To warn against false teachers and affirm the certainty of Christ's coming

1 John.author: Traditionally John the apostle
1 John.setting: Secessionists denying Jesus came in the flesh
1 John.purpose: To give assurance of eternal life through tests of belief, obedience and love

2 John.author: 'The elder' (John)
2 John.audience: 'The elect lady and her children' (a church)
2 John.purpose: To urge love in truth and refuse hospitality to deceivers

3 John.author: 'The elder' (John)
3 John.purpose: To commend Gaius' hospitality and rebuke Diotrephes

Jude.author: Jude, brother of James and of Jesus
Jude.setting: Libertine false teachers infiltrating the church
Jude.purpose: To contend for the faith once delivered to the saints

Revelation.author: John (the apostle, per tradition), on Patmos
Revelation.date: c. AD 96 (Ussher); others c. AD 95 or c. AD 68
Revelation.setting: Roman imperial cult; persecution under Domitian (or Nero)
Revelation.purpose: To unveil Jesus Christ as the risen Lord of history and encourage faithful endurance until the new creation
